lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: October 1st, 2013. San Francisco. A quiet public library.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In the science fiction section, a 29-year-old in a T-shirt is typing on his laptop.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He looks like a grad student. He is actually running the biggest black market on the internet. A site that, according to the FBI, did 1.2 billion dollars in sales.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Behind him, a man and a woman start a loud argument. He turns around, for just one second.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And that one second ends everything. But to understand why, we have to go back.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: This is the story of Ross Ulbricht, and the Silk Road.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Austin, Texas. Ross Ulbricht is born in 1984. Smart, friendly, and an actual Eagle Scout.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He studies physics, then earns a master's degree in materials science. Crystals, mostly.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But Ross doesn't want a lab job. He wants freedom. He reads libertarian economics, and starts believing governments shouldn't control what people buy or sell.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He tries day trading. It fails. He starts a video game company. That fails too. He sells used books online. Honestly? Also not great.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So in 2010, he has a new idea. A website where anyone can buy anything, completely anonymously.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He names it Silk Road, after the ancient trade route between China and Europe.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The trick is two pieces of technology. Tor hides where users are. And Bitcoin, a brand new digital currency, hides who's paying.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Tor works like an onion. Your traffic is wrapped in layers of encryption and bounced around the world, so no one can tell where it came from.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Back then, one bitcoin was worth about a dollar. Keep that in mind.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: To get the first products on the site, Ross grows magic mushrooms himself, in a cabin outside Austin.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: February 2011. Silk Road goes live. It looks like a normal online shop, with listings, reviews and star ratings. Except most of the listings are illegal drugs.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Sellers get star ratings. Buyers leave reviews. There is even customer support.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Somewhere out there, a drug dealer is getting five stars for fast shipping and lovely packaging.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: To spread the word, he posts about it on online forums, under the username altoid. Remember that name.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In June 2011, a news site publishes a story about Silk Road. Overnight, everyone knows. A US senator demands it be shut down.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Which, as free advertising goes, is pretty hard to beat.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The site explodes. Thousands of sellers. Nearly a million user accounts.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ross takes a new name: Dread Pirate Roberts. It comes from the movie The Princess Bride, where the name is passed from one pirate to the next. So nobody knows who's really behind it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He takes a cut of every sale. By the FBI's count, the site moves 9.5 million bitcoins in sales, and earns about 80 million dollars in commissions.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He tracks the money in detailed spreadsheets, like any good small business owner. Except this business is not small, and not legal.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And here's the strange part. The boss of this empire lives in a rented room in San Francisco, paying a thousand dollars a month in cash, under a fake name: Josh.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His roommates think he's a quiet guy who works on his computer all day. Which, to be fair, was true.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But Silk Road was not a harmless game. Prosecutors linked six overdose deaths to drugs bought on the site, and grieving parents spoke at his sentencing.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Prosecutors also said he paid to have people killed to protect the site. No one was actually harmed, and he was never convicted on those claims.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Meanwhile, the hunt is on. The FBI, the DEA, Homeland Security and the IRS are all chasing one pirate.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And the breakthrough doesn't come from hackers or spy satellites. It comes from Google.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: An IRS agent named Gary Alford searches for the oldest posts that mention Silk Road. And he finds altoid.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Later, altoid had posted again, asking for a programmer. And for replies, he left his email address: rossulbricht at gmail dot com.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His real name. In his email. On the internet. The Dread Pirate, ladies and gentlemen.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: It gets better. He also asked a coding question online under his real name, then changed his username to frosty. Less than a minute later. The internet remembers.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then, in July 2013, border agents open a package from Canada. Inside: nine fake IDs. Different names. Same face. All addressed to Ross's apartment.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Homeland Security knocks on his door. Ross admits nothing. But he does mention that, hypothetically, anyone could buy fake IDs on a site called Silk Road.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Hypothetically.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Now the agents have a name. But a name isn't enough. Everything is on his laptop, and if that laptop closes, it's locked and encrypted.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: They need to grab it while it's open, while he's logged in as the Dread Pirate.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: October 1st, 2013. An undercover agent, who has secretly taken over a Silk Road staff account, starts chatting with the boss.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ross walks into a cafe. Too crowded. So he walks next door, to the Glen Park library.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He sits down in the science fiction section, opens his laptop, and logs in.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The undercover agent asks him to check something on the site's admin page. Ross opens it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Behind him, two FBI agents start their act: a loud lovers' fight. Ross turns to look.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In that second, another agent slides the open laptop away. Screen on. Logged in. Game over.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Lesson of the day: always lock your laptop.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: On it, agents find everything. Chat logs. Spreadsheets of profits. Even a personal diary describing how he started Silk Road.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He wrote down his crimes. In a diary. On the evidence.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Agents also seize about 144,000 bitcoins from his computer. Back then, about 28 million dollars. Today, worth billions.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And Silk Road itself? Just one month later, copycats launch Silk Road 2.0. Shut down the next year. The internet, it turns out, is very good at copying.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In February 2015, a jury in New York finds him guilty on all seven counts.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: In May, the judge sentences him to two life sentences, plus forty years. No parole.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But this story has one more twist. Two of the federal agents investigating Silk Road were stealing bitcoin themselves.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: A DEA agent took bitcoin from Ross while pretending to be someone else. A Secret Service agent stole over 800,000 dollars in bitcoin from the site.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Both went to prison. The investigators needed investigating.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And another hacker who tricked Silk Road out of 50,000 bitcoins hid them for almost ten years. Agents finally found them in 2021, on a tiny computer inside a popcorn tin, in a bathroom closet.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Worth more than 3 billion dollars. The most expensive popcorn in history.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ross spends more than eleven years in prison. Supporters campaign to free him. Critics say the sentence fit the crime.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Then, on January 21st, 2025, President Trump grants him a full and unconditional pardon. He walks out a free man.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Months later, he's on stage at a Bitcoin conference, in front of a cheering crowd.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: So who is Ross Ulbricht? A freedom fighter, or a kingpin? People still argue about it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But one thing is certain. The man who built the internet's most secret marketplace was caught by a Google search, a box of fake IDs, and a fake argument in a library.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: This was Unfiled Films. Should he have been pardoned? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more stories like this.
